name: Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) extract
short: Review: linked to bleeding in people on anticoagulants. Colitis: serious adverse events rare in a small trial, none in a 13-person pilot (disease rose after stopping); none severe in office workers.
text: In an 8-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a dietary supplement containing bilberry extract, taken as a daily capsule, in office workers aged 20 to 40 (88 enrolled; the abstract does not say whether the supplement contained other ingredients), adverse events were collected through medical interviews and there were no severe adverse events in either group. In an open pilot study in 13 people with mild to moderate ulcerative colitis who took a standardised anthocyanin-rich bilberry preparation daily for 6 weeks, no serious adverse events were observed, but calprotectin levels (a gut inflammation marker) and disease activity increased after bilberry intake was stopped. In a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of an anthocyanin-rich extract of bilberries in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, which ended early with 34 patients randomised, serious adverse events were rare; the abstract does not give their number or compare them between groups. A 2022 literature review of dietary supplements and bleeding lists bilberry among the supplements associated with bleeding risk in people taking anticoagulants (blood thinners). It found no evidence of bleeding with these supplements in people not taking anticoagulants. The abstract does not give the type of evidence or the number of cases for bilberry.
